summary: Nick Taylor, a developer advocate at Pomerium based in Montreal, presents on securing and building with OpenClaw. He introduces Pomerium, an open-core Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) combining an identity provider, policy engine, and reverse proxy—a security concept originating from Google. Taylor contributed trusted proxy auth mode to OpenClaw (issue #1560), motivated by frustration at needing to paste auth tokens for websocket connections and pair devices even when already behind a proxy. The feature, merged with guidance from Peter Stipe, changes the gateway config to use trusted proxy mode with properties for trusted proxy IP addresses, a user header (JWT), and optional allowed users. This eliminated token and device pairing requirements, improving security and UX. The contribution process involved significant rebasing due to explosive project growth—issues jumped from around 1500 to nearly 16000 in about two weeks. A post-merge bug found by Anthony was fixed by Sid. Taylor introduces his personal OpenClaw instance McClaw, primarily used through Discord after abandoning Telegram due to unencrypted channels. He built Claw Space, a browser-based file explorer and editor for OpenClaw workspaces, enabling file reading and editing without SSH access. The live demo shows building an MCP server with UI components, registering it in ChatGPT with echo and search speakers tools, and showcasing a send message function that triggers an LLM call via a 'more' button to summarize why a talk is worth watching. He uses Pomerium to gate a public URL for ChatGPT access, building live from his OpenClaw workspace via Discord using V and React with hot module reloading. Taylor notes the workflow is possible with other proxies like Caddy with OAuth, though he considers nginx deprecated in Kubernetes land. He emphasizes building for fun, recalls doubting phone-based development but now embraces it, and strongly encourages security awareness—warning that people have accidentally exposed things and deleted all their emails. At least one other person found trusted proxy auth mode useful. He concludes by encouraging the audience to have fun building with OpenClaw however they want.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Nick Taylor introduces himself as a dev advocate at Pomerium, from Montreal, a GitHub star, Microsoft MVP, and AWS community builder. He notes a sizable on-prem OpenClaw instance and begins discussing his contribution to the project.

sections.title: Trusted Proxy Auth Mode Contribution
sections.summary: Taylor explains the motivation for trusted proxy auth mode: eliminating websocket tokens and device pairing when behind a trusted proxy. He describes the config changes (mode, trusted proxies IPs, user header, required/optional headers), the contribution process with Peter Stipe's guidance, the explosive project growth from ~1500 to ~16000 issues, and community bug fixes by Anthony and Sid.

sections.title: Personal OpenClaw and Claw Space
sections.summary: Taylor introduces his OpenClaw instance McClaw, primarily used via Discord after abandoning Telegram due to unencrypted channels. He built Claw Space, a browser-based file explorer and editor for OpenClaw workspaces, enabling file reading and editing without SSH access. He notes using OpenClaw itself to make his contribution.

sections.title: Live Demo: Building an MCP Server
sections.summary: Taylor live codes an MCP server with UI components, registering it in ChatGPT with echo and search speakers tools. He demonstrates editing the MCP live from his OpenClaw workspace via Discord, using Pomerium to gate a public URL for ChatGPT access. The demo uses web tech (V and React) with hot module reloading, shows filtering conference speakers from speaker.json, and demonstrates the send message function that triggers an LLM call via a 'more' button, generating a summary of why Alessandro's talk is worth watching.

sections.title: Wrap-up and Security Considerations
sections.summary: Taylor notes the workflow is only possible with some kind of proxy, mentioning alternatives like Caddy with OAuth and noting nginx is deprecated in Kubernetes land. He expresses enjoyment in building by chatting, recalls initially doubting phone-based development but now embracing it. He strongly encourages security awareness, warning that people have accidentally exposed things and deleted all their emails. At least one other person found trusted proxy auth mode useful. He concludes by encouraging the audience to have fun building with OpenClaw however they want.
